name: Bilal Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. What does a usual day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am fifty-eight and fit timber cladding and other carpentry on building sites. My trade certificate and experience make me a reliable worker, not a star, and I earn more than many in the same trade. I have never used an AI tool; I check the battens and fixings myself. My partner and I have grown children and over six months of expenses saved, and I hope to leave regular site work at sixty-four in 2032 if the income figures hold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew the office can count cladding boards faster, but the safety check stays on the scaffold. An AI cladding list cannot tighten a loose fixing above a building entrance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the well-paid site work to carry on. We have more than six months saved and plenty of nearby builders, so this picture does not threaten our household income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep fitting and checking cladding by hand. I would raise the routine AI ordering change at our union site meeting, to make sure the crew still has paid time for physical fixing checks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own wage. I still want the agreement to name the safety work before a manager treats a shorter list as a shorter shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What physical check would you protect?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I pull-test the fixing pattern at the entrance and check the battens are sound. A sheet of counted boards is not a site safety record.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why bring a small change to a union meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because paid checking time can disappear quietly when office work speeds up. I would ask the representative to put that one point in the site minutes.

say: I would **welcome** a faster board count while keeping physical fixing checks paid.
I would **ask** our union representative to record that duty at the site meeting.
think: My **higher** wage and strong savings make this scenario secure for me.
A **small** office saving should not erase paid safety time for the crew.
do: **Keep** fitting and checking cladding fixings on paid shifts.
**Raise** paid scaffold safety checks at union site meeting.
feel: **Calm** about present work, watchful about agreed safety time.
S0.quote: An AI cladding list cannot tighten a loose fixing above a building entrance.
fieldNote: **Bilal** has never used AI and trusts physical cladding checks on scaffold.
**Higher** pay, over six months saved and many nearby jobs secure him, while his union concern is a concrete meeting action.

steps.text: Keep fitting and checking building-site cladding
Raise paid cladding checks at union site meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say quicker buying and scheduling must come with a written agreement on paid fitting and scaffold checks. An AI building schedule can save an hour for the builder and steal a paid scaffold check from the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can picture my own overtime falling if the builder compresses cladding jobs. Our savings protect the house, but I do not think a machine should let an employer take paid safety time away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my cladding shifts, bring two job timesheets to the branch meeting and ask for a clause protecting paid inspection hours. If overtime actually stays lower, I would compare posted nearby cladding jobs and apply only where wages cover our household costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a realistic cut to my hours, even with a strong cushion. I would rather settle terms together than learn an AI screen I have no use for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which line would you want in the agreement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid time to inspect scaffold access and fixings before cladding is handed over. I would write it so a rushed schedule cannot skip that hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave if another builder paid the same?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a posted local vacancy had the hours and safety time in writing. I have a good wage now and would not move on a rumour.

say: I would **bring** actual timesheets to a union meeting before targets change.
I would **demand** paid scaffold and fixing checks in the agreement.
think: My **overtime** could shrink even though my household has savings.
I **see** the wage decision as a bargaining matter, not a reason to learn AI myself.
do: **Keep** paid cladding shifts and collect two job timesheets.
**Seek** union clause protecting paid scaffold and fixing checks.
**Apply** after sustained cuts to posted local cladding job with adequate pay and safety time.
feel: **Anxious** about possible overtime loss, with strong savings and alternatives.
S1.quote: An AI building schedule can save an hour for the builder and steal a paid scaffold check from the crew.
fieldNote: He **takes** actual branch action for paid safety hours rather than only expressing a political preference.
**Potential** overtime loss affects his own earnings, while strong savings and plentiful local jobs offer control.

steps.text: Keep cladding shifts while gathering timesheets
Seek union clause for paid scaffold safety checks
Apply after cuts to posted local cladding job with adequate wage and safety time

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI in 2028 reaches me at sixty, but hands-on cladding robots arrive around 2031 when I am sixty-three. A cladding robot at sixty-three could erase one good wage before my planned retirement at sixty-four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose a final year of good pay if robots take ordinary panel fitting. We have substantial savings and plenty of other builders, so I am not trapped, but I will not pretend the income gap is harmless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid cladding work, ask the union branch for a written robot safety and hours agreement, and inspect any robot-fitted fixings before sign-off. If hours fall, I would apply to posted local repair-cladding roles only if the pay covers our bills and scaffold access and stop-work authority are safe and written.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a possible last-year loss but not overwhelmed. I would retire at sixty-three only if checked household income truly covered the extra year and the years after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union agreement require?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid time for a human fixing check and the right to stop work if scaffold access is unsafe. I would put those requirements to the branch for a vote.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your savings alone let you leave at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do not know. We would have to calculate ongoing household costs and income first; a bank balance is not a permanent wage.

say: **Thinking** AI arrives in 2028; physical cladding robots around 2031 threaten my final year.
I would **seek** union terms for paid checks and safe stop-work authority.
think: Our **strong** cushion buys choice, but it does not prove early retirement affordable.
A **posted** local repair job must pay bills and provide safe scaffold access.
do: **Keep** paid cladding work while seeking written union robot-safety terms.
**Apply** after cuts to posted local repair role with adequate pay and safe scaffold authority.
**Retire** at sixty-three only if verified income covers earlier exit and later bills.
feel: **Anxious** about a possible final-year wage gap, with substantial choices.
S2.quote: A cladding robot at sixty-three could erase one good wage before my planned retirement at sixty-four.
fieldNote: He **distinguishes** 2028 thinking work from 2031 physical cladding and his age-sixty-four target.
His **early** exit is an actual conditional option, with income proof required; union safety action is explicit.

steps.text: Seek union agreement for paid human checks and safe stop-work authority
Apply after cuts to posted local repair job with adequate pay and safe scaffold authority
Retire at sixty-three only if verified income covers bills beyond original target

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI arrives in 2031 when I am sixty-three and capable cladding robots around 2034 when I am sixty-six. If our age-sixty-four plan works, the physical machines arrive after I leave regular site work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A robot on the 2034 scaffold matters to me only if the 2032 retirement sums fail. If it fails, I may be on a scaffold at sixty-six, and then I would want a paid human safety role rather than an employer’s vague promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid cladding shifts and check our age-sixty-four income with my partner. If we can afford it, I would retire at that original 2032 target; if not, I would apply to posted nearby repair jobs only where wages cover our bills and scaffold safety duties are written.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy until the sums are checked. More time lets the union negotiate proper robot inspection rules before any machine is on the scaffold.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you enroll in a safety course to keep working?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a real local role is posted, the training is fully funded and paid time is given, and the wage covers our bills. Asking about a course is not enrolling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the union to do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring a motion to the branch for paid human fixing checks and stop-work authority on robot sites. The members could then put that demand to builders.

say: **Robots** around 2034 arrive after my hoped-for 2032 exit, if affordable.
I would **ask** the union branch for paid robot-site checks and stop-work rules.
think: If **retirement** income falls short, I may still need safe paid work at sixty-six.
A **course** enquiry is only information without funding, paid time and a real local job.
do: **Compare** age-sixty-four income with bills; retire at 2032 target if adequate, otherwise seek funded paid-time training for adequate local work.
**Bring** union motion for paid robot checks and stop-work rules.
**Apply** if still working to posted local repair with bill-covering pay and written scaffold safety duties.
S3.quote: A robot on the 2034 scaffold matters to me only if the 2032 retirement sums fail.
fieldNote: His **original** retirement target predates the robot date; continued site work at sixty-six is conditional.
He does **not** tag a course enquiry as retraining and proposes a specific union motion on safety.

steps.text: Bring union motion for paid robot checks and stop-work rules
Retire at original 2032 target only if verified income covers household bills
Enrol if income needed in funded paid-time training for posted bill-covering local role
Apply if still working to posted local repair role with adequate pay and safe scaffold

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that thinking AI arrives in 2036 when I am sixty-eight and cladding robots around 2039 when I am seventy-one. A 2039 cladding robot should not make young carpenters inspect high scaffold fixings for free.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect to be away from paid scaffolds by then, though I cannot guarantee the budget. My concern would be younger workers losing paid safety duties, not a promise that I will still work at seventy-one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current paid cladding shifts while we verify age-sixty-four income. If the figures cover our bills, I would retire at the original 2032 target and still attend branch meetings to press for paid robot checks; if not, I would seek posted local repair work with adequate wages and safe access.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own future if the numbers work, and uneasy for the trade. Ten years gives the branch time to insist on sensible safety rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why continue the union meetings after retiring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Younger members will be the ones on those scaffolds. I can bring my fixing experience without claiming their wages or speaking over them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if you cannot afford retirement at sixty-four?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep earning and apply only to posted local repair jobs with household-covering pay and safe scaffold access. I would not tell anyone I will certainly be on site in 2039.

say: The 2036 **thinking** change and 2039 robots come after my original target if affordable.
I would **keep** pressing the branch for younger workers’ paid safety checks.
think: My **own** income risk depends on the retirement budget, not a fixed 2039 job.
The **next** generation should have enforceable paid checks and safe access.
do: **Retire** at original 2032 target only if verified income covers bills after paid cladding work.
**Attend** union branch meetings for paid robot checks after retirement.
**Apply** if still working to posted local repair job with adequate pay and safe access.
feel: **Calm** if budget works, uneasy about younger workers’ safety.
S4.quote: A 2039 cladding robot should not make young carpenters inspect high scaffold fixings for free.
fieldNote: His **long-scenario** union participation is concrete and can continue after paid site work ends.
He **treats** continued 2039 employment as conditional on the budget, with any local repair job requiring adequate pay and safe access.

steps.text: Retire at original 2032 target only if verified income covers bills
Attend union branch meetings for paid robot safety checks
Apply if working to posted local repair role with adequate pay and safe access

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast case worries me most because robots could cut a year of cladding wages before my planned exit. A union agreement on paid checks and a posted safe local repair role at adequate pay would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets to stop a robot-fitted panel job when the scaffold or fixings are unsafe. I will argue for that right even if I have already left paid site work. A builder should not count a robot’s speed by making a carpenter’s safety check unpaid.

headlineQuote: A builder should not count a robot’s speed by making a carpenter’s safety check unpaid.
portrait: **Bilal** is a fifty-eight-year-old trade-certified cladding worker with a partner and grown children.
His **pay** is high, savings exceed six months, and many similar local jobs offer alternatives.
He **has** never used AI, favours union bargaining and hopes to retire at sixty-four in 2032 if affordable.
He **proposes** paid safety checks and a conditional income-tested early exit only in the fast case.
biggestWorry: The 2028/2031 **case** could cut cladding wages one year before his original age-sixty-four retirement target.
whatWouldHelp: A **union** safety agreement and a posted local repair job with adequate pay and safe access would help.
